Me Magnets™ — Instructions

An Identity & Self-Expression Tool

Me Magnets help individuals, families, and couples identify, explore, and express core values and various parts of identity.

General use

Focus on one color category at a time. Choose magnets that you feel accurately describe you. Drag or click each word to move it to your collection. Click it again to return it. For purple, consider narrowing your choices to the 6–8 values most important to you; this is optional.

View your completed collection under “SHOW ME!” Couples, parents, and families can share chosen magnets to spark meaningful conversations and learn more about their loved ones. Share, save, or print only with permission.

Color categories

The orange and pink word collections are optional. Use the checkmark buttons at the top of the game to include or hide Feelings and Gender & Sexuality. Turning a category off hides its magnets but preserves your selections. The original physical kit also includes blank magnets for making your own words.

For qualified mental health professionals only

Families and couples

Use Me Magnets to identify and explore values that may be at the root of miscommunication, misunderstandings, or ongoing resentments. Identifying and communicating core values can increase empathy and understanding. Have participants choose 6–8 important values, share them, and identify which are compatible or may be in conflict. Prompt for real-life examples of how conflicting values may have contributed to an argument, misunderstanding, or resentment.

Self-esteem

After the client chooses their magnets, focus on the red and blue collections. Red magnets shed light on negative self-images or beliefs. Explore the roots of these beliefs, possible cognitive distortions, and other self-esteem challenges. Use selected blue magnets to validate positive qualities. If the client has difficulty identifying blue magnets, offer some that you feel describe them.

Teens

Use Me Magnets to help teens navigate personality and identity development as they become more independent from caregivers. Teens can explore aspects of personality and select words that represent them. With their permission, sharing these selections with a therapist or caregiver can support identity exploration, rapport, and expression of emotional material to adults.
